extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, and researchers interested in Hungarian politics and academic misconduct
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic account of the Pál Schmitt plagiarism controversy summarizing allegations, identified sources, investigatory procedures, institutional responses, and outcomes related to an alleged doctoral-thesis plagiarism case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dr. univ. versus PhD (degree standard and conversion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Until 1993 the only doctoral title Hungarian universities could award was the doctor universitatis, or dr. univ., title. It was not considered to be an academic degree. The requirements for the univ. dr. title were generally below the Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) requirements. In 1993, the PhD degree was introduced in Hungary, and the universities had the jurisdiction to convert dr. univ. degrees to PhD doctorates on a case-by-case basis, if they met the necessary requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Background standard: a dr. univ. has different (lower) formal requirements than a PhD; conversion is discretionary and evaluated case-by-case by universities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism / originality requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting a thesis written by someone else as one's own work constitutes a criminal offence. The fact-finding committee found that large portions (197 pages / ~180 pages) of Schmitt's dissertation were verbatim copies or direct translations from other works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantial verbatim copying or close translation without proper attribution is treated as plagiarism and may trigger academic and legal consequences; degree revocation is possible when originality is not met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation practice and in-text attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The dissertation did not contain in-body citations, only a bibliography listing. The report asserts the author did not indicate his sources anywhere in the thesis (uses neither quotation marks, nor author names in parentheses, nor footnotes, nor endnotes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarly work should use explicit in-text citation mechanisms (quotation marks, parentheses, footnotes/endnotes) to indicate direct quotations and source use rather than relying solely on a bibliography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibliography accuracy and completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: The bibliography contained errors (place of publication of Georgiev's manuscript was incorrectly given; 5 out of 21 cited references could not be identified; out of 23 self-citations, 10 could not be found, and 3 were cited wrongly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bibliographic entries must be accurate and traceable (correct titles, publication places, languages); missing or incorrect bibliographic information undermines the scholarly validity of the thesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of quotation marks / marking direct quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: The text uses neither quotation marks, nor author names in parentheses, nor footnotes, nor endnotes to indicate direct quotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct quotations must be clearly marked and attributed; failure to mark quotations is a formal defect contributing to findings of plagiarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgments of collaborators/support
rubrics_metrics.description: The thesis does not contain any acknowledgments of support from collaborators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theses should acknowledge collaborators and sources of assistance where appropriate to make contributions and provenance clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution of figures, tables and appendices
rubrics_metrics.description: The seven tables and two charts that make up the appendix were taken from Georgiev's manuscript without proper attribution; figure 1 was a photocopy of a figure in Georgiev's work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All figures, tables and appended material not original to the candidate must be clearly credited to their sources; copying figures/tables without attribution is an academic integrity violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis committee conflict-of-interest rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The 37th section of the 1985 Doctoral Regulations stated that 'a person from whom an objective assessment of the candidate's work cannot be expected may not participate in review of the doctoral dissertation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee members should be impartial and not have organizational ties to the candidate that would prevent objective assessment; membership of thesis reviewers in organizations headed by the candidate raises conflict-of-interest concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervisor/examiner responsibility to detect and alert on citation issues
rubrics_metrics.description: The report faults the thesis advisor and the examiners for not alerting the candidate to the inappropriate or absent citations, which are largely typical of the thesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advisors and examiners have a duty to check citation practices and notify candidates of formal or substantive deficiencies; failure to do so may implicate supervisors in procedural shortcomings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required procedural documentation for degree conferral
rubrics_metrics.description: Missing documents imply formal irregularities: the thesis proposal, the report on the comprehensive examination, and the minutes of the thesis committee could not be found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universities should maintain complete records (proposal, examination reports, committee minutes) demonstrating that proper procedures were followed in awarding degrees; absence of such documents calls procedure into question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and pacing of thesis procedures (defense timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The defense took place barely a month after registration—a conspicuous (although not necessarily against the regulations) timing noted by the report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequate time between registration, research, and defense is expected; unusually rapid progression to defense can indicate procedural irregularity or insufficient review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent-of-copying threshold for unacceptable work
rubrics_metrics.description: The thesis is based on a word-by-word translation of 'unusually large extent,' which should have been detected at the defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large-scale verbatim translation or copying (beyond acceptable quotation and fair use) is unacceptable and should lead to remedial or punitive measures including degree revocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: University's duty to ensure compliance with contemporaneous regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The report concluded that the thesis procedure was, notwithstanding the procedural shortcomings, in accordance with the practices of the University of Physical Education at the time, but also faults the university for leading the author to believe the thesis met the requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universities must ensure that degree-awarding practices meet both formal regulations and scholarly standards; institutional oversight is responsible for preventing and addressing misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction for investigating alleged misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: An investigation needs to be conducted by the university that issued the title; the Hungarian Accreditation Committee stated that the university should investigate the allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary investigatory jurisdiction over thesis-related misconduct lies with the issuing institution, subject to oversight or validation by accreditation bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of external experts in sensitive/politically charged investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: The university explored asking experts from outside the country to examine the dissertation because local experts qualified to be members were turning down requests, apparently due to the politically sensitive nature of the issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When local impartiality or willingness is compromised, institutions should appoint external experts to ensure credible, unbiased assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent, fair and public investigation expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Seven scholars started a petition asking for a fair, public and transparent investigation of the allegations; they argued failing to investigate would 'becloud every scientific degree...and discredit institutions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations into alleged academic misconduct should be conducted transparently and fairly to preserve institutional credibility and public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative mechanisms for revoking degrees
rubrics_metrics.description: The University Council advised the University Senate to withdraw Schmitt's doctorate title; the University Senate voted to withdraw the title (33–4) and the doctoral council initiated proceedings for revocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universities have administrative procedures (councils, senates, doctoral councils) to evaluate and, if warranted, revoke academic degrees when standards are not met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential criminal/administrative consequences for thesis fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: The State Secretariat for Education reminded students that submitting a thesis written by someone else as one's own work constitutes a criminal offence and that the Ministry would file a complaint with the National Police Headquarters if aware of thesis-related abuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In addition to academic sanctions, thesis fraud can trigger criminal or administrative investigations initiated by governmental authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of accreditation/oversight bodies to validate university decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: On 2 April the president of the Hungarian Accreditation Committee announced that the decision of the University Senate was legitimate according to relevant regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accreditation bodies may review or endorse university decisions on misconduct and degree revocation to ensure conformity with regulations and standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly ethical standards and professional recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Klaus Heinemann expressed concern that misuse of his work harmed his scientific recognition; commentators referenced 'basic and essential ethical norms of science.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Academic work must conform to ethical norms protecting authorship, attribution and the integrity of scholarly recognition; violations damage individual reputations and the field's credibility.
